document.title: Quality Appraisal AI — Framework Overview
document.abstract: A walkthrough of the architecture, prompts, and scoring logic behind the Quality Appraisal feature, written for AI engineers who want to understand the building blocks and adapt portions to their own systems. Prompts are shown verbatim and scoring algorithms are presented as pseudocode and flowcharts.

section.title: What the system does
section.paragraph: Given a single clinical research paper (PDF), the system produces a structured quality-of-evidence assessment:

steps.step: Classifies the study design (RCT, cohort, meta-analysis, …).
Extracts structured fields (citation, population, outcomes, design modifiers).
Picks the primary outcome automatically from the extracted fields.
Runs a validated risk-of-bias tool for that study type (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2 for RCTs).
Runs a reporting-guideline checklist (e.g., CONSORT 2025 for RCTs).
Computes a GRADE certainty level (initial, based on study type; updated, after risk-of-bias).

section.paragraph: v1 ships with RCT support only. The architecture is a registry pattern so new study-type / tool / guideline tuples can be added as three-line entries plus two small modules.

section.title: Pipeline (per paper)

pipeline.stage: Extract structured fields (universal + type-specific + design modifiers)
Risk of bias (RoB 2) — one call per domain + Python decision trees

section.paragraph: Total: ~8 LLM calls per paper. Batch isolation is enforced so one bad PDF never blocks the run; failures and unsupported study types are logged per paper and the run continues.

section.title: Extensibility contract
section.paragraph: The whole system is driven by a single registry table keyed by study type:
Each tool and guideline lives in its own module and exposes two entrypoints:

Adding a new study type is: one registry entry, one rob_tools/<name>.py, one reporting_guidelines/<name>.py, one dispatcher registration. That's it. Registry keys must match the classifier's study-type labels; we enforce that with a unit test.

section.title: LLM interaction pattern
section.paragraph: All AI calls funnel through a single oversize-robust function (called _call_with_pdf in our code). Conceptually:

Classification and schema-proposal calls short-circuit to first-chunk-only (chunking a single holistic output doesn't make sense). All error paths surface vendor-agnostic 4xx/5xx messages. A hard 32 MB byte-size guard runs before we even base64-encode, since the underlying PDF-beta endpoint rejects larger payloads.

section.title: Risk of Bias — Cochrane RoB 2 (2019, parallel-group RCTs)

subsection.title: Design choice: LLM answers, Python judges
subsection.paragraph: RoB 2 has five domains. Each domain has 3–7 signaling questions answered with Y / PY / PN / N / NI (yes / probably-yes / probably-no / no / no-information). The Cochrane cribsheet defines a fixed flowchart mapping signal answers to a domain judgement (Low / Some concerns / High).

split.role: Answers signaling questions from the paper text (subjective, paper-dependent).
Maps those answers to judgements (deterministic, auditable).

subsection.paragraph: Keeping the flowcharts in code means the developer-transparency view can show the exact logic via inspect.getsource — reviewers can see there is no hidden LLM arbitration step.

subsection.title: System prompt (verbatim)
subsection.prompt: You are an evidence-synthesis methodologist assessing risk of bias in a randomized trial using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Read the PDF carefully. Answer each signaling question with one of: Y (yes), PY (probably yes), PN (probably no), N (no), NI (no information). Provide a 1-2 sentence rationale for each answer, quoting the paper where possible. Return ONLY a valid JSON object — no preamble, no markdown fences.

subsection.title: Per-domain prompt template (verbatim)
subsection.paragraph: One call per domain. The template below is filled in with the study type, the primary outcome (RoB 2 is outcome-specific), structured fields already extracted from the paper, and the domain's signaling questions + the verbatim cribsheet elaborations.

notes.note: For each domain, only the relevant extracted fields are passed in, not the whole extraction. That keeps the prompt focused and reminds the model what we already know (e.g., Domain 1 gets randomization_method, allocation_concealment, baseline_balance, …).
RoB 2 is assessed per-outcome, so the primary outcome is always in the header. A future version with user-selectable outcomes would loop this step.
Captured alongside each domain in case reviewers want to aggregate "which way does the bias point" across a body of evidence.

subsection.title: Decision trees (pseudocode)
subsection.paragraph: The five domain algorithms are transcribed directly from the 2019 cribsheet. Below are the flowcharts in pseudocode — enough to understand the structure, not verbatim Python.
subsection.code: yes(a) := a ∈ {Y, PY} no(a) := a ∈ {N, PN}
subsection.decision-tree: if no(1.2): return High # allocation not concealed if 1.2 == NI: return High if yes(1.3) else Some concerns # no info on concealment # 1.2 is Y/PY if no(1.1): return High # sequence not random # 1.1 is Y/PY/NI, 1.2 is Y/PY return Some concerns if yes(1.3) else Low # 1.3 flags baseline imbalance

decision-tree.title: Deviations from intended interventions, effect of assignment

subsection.decision-tree: if yes(3.1): return Low # data for (nearly) all if yes(3.2): return Low # evidence result not biased if no(3.3): return Low # missingness can't depend on true value # 3.3 is Y/PY/NI → 3.4 likely depended? if yes(3.4) or 3.4 == NI: return High return Some concerns

if yes(4.1): return High # inappropriate method if yes(4.2): return High # measurement differs between groups # Aware-of-assignment chain base = { if no(4.3): → Low elif no(4.4): → Low elif yes(4.5) or 4.5 == NI: → High else: → Some concerns } # NI on 4.2 downgrades a Low to Some concerns if 4.2 == NI and base == Low: return Some concerns return base

if yes(5.2) or yes(5.3): return High # cherry-picked measurement or analysis if no(5.2) and no(5.3): return Low if yes(5.1) else Some concerns # pre-specified analysis plan? return Some concerns # at least one NI
if any(domain == High): return High if count(domain == Some concerns) >= 2: return High # ≥2 "somes" aggregate to High if count(domain == Some concerns) >= 1: return Some concerns return Low

subsection.title: Signaling questions at a glance
subsection.paragraph: Domain count is fixed by the tool: 5 domains, 22 signaling questions (3 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 3). Question wording and elaborations are transcribed verbatim from 20190814_RoB_2.0_cribsheet_parallel_trial.pdf and sent to the LLM unchanged so it sees the same guidance a human reviewer would.

question.elaboration_gist: Random-number tables/computers/coin flips count; alternation/DOB/ record-# do not; "randomized" alone = NI.

question.text: Was the allocation sequence concealed until assignment?
question.elaboration_gist: Central pharmacy / sequentially-numbered tamper-sealed opaque envelopes count.

question.text: Did baseline differences suggest a problem with randomization?
question.elaboration_gist: Chance imbalance is fine; flag substantial imbalance in prognostic factors.

subsection.paragraph: The remaining four domains follow the same pattern; the full text is shipped in the developer-view endpoint so any engineer on a reviewing team can audit what the LLM sees.

section.title: Reporting guideline — CONSORT 2025
section.paragraph: CONSORT 2025 is a 30-item checklist. Unlike RoB 2, we make a single LLM call covering all items — they're independent and each is a short yes/no with evidence, so there's no scoring logic that needs to be isolated from the model.

subsection.title: System prompt (verbatim)
subsection.prompt: You are an evidence-synthesis methodologist assessing adherence of a randomised trial report to the CONSORT 2025 checklist. Read the PDF carefully. For each checklist item, decide whether the trial report reports the required information. Be strict but fair: an item is adhered only if the information is actually present (not merely referenced as 'available elsewhere' unless the paper provides a usable pointer). If an item is genuinely not applicable to this trial, mark it N/A. Return ONLY a valid JSON object — no preamble, no markdown fences.

subsection.title: User prompt template (verbatim)
Scoring (pseudocode)
subsection.code:
# Inputs: 30 item judgements from the LLM, each {adhered: true|false|null, evidence: str} applicable = [it for it in items if it.adhered is not None] adhered = count(it.adhered == true for it in applicable) proportion = adhered / len(applicable) if applicable else 0.0
return { items: items, adhered: adhered, applicable: len(applicable), total: 30, proportion: proportion, }
subsection.paragraph: Not-applicable items are excluded from both numerator and denominator so they don't inflate or deflate the proportion (e.g., 16b interim analyses for a trial that had none). Non-boolean returns from the LLM are coerced defensively ("yes"/"true"/"1" → True, "na"/"none" → None, everything else → None).
subsection.citation: Hopewell S et al. "CONSORT 2025 Statement: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials." BMJ 2025; 388:e081123. https://dx.doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-081123

section.title: GRADE certainty
section.paragraph: GRADE has five domains in full: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias. Four of them require a body of evidence (heterogeneity between studies, wide vs narrow confidence intervals across studies, funnel-plot asymmetry) and so don't apply to a single-study assessment.
v1 downgrades for risk of bias only.

subsection.title: Initial GRADE
subsection.paragraph: Assigned by study type from the registry. RCTs start at High; observational designs start at Low (standard GRADE convention).

subsection.title: Downgrade rule (pseudocode)
subsection.code:
levels = [High, Moderate, Low, Very low] i = index(initial)
if rob_overall == Low: return initial, "No downgrade: overall risk of bias is Low." if rob_overall == Some concerns: return levels[min(i+1, 3)], "Downgraded 1 level for Some concerns in risk of bias." # rob_overall == High high_domains = count(d == High for d in rob_domain_judgements) if high_domains >= 2: return levels[min(i+2, 3)], f"Downgraded 2 levels for High risk of bias in {high_domains} domains." return levels[min(i+1, 3)], "Downgraded 1 level for High risk of bias."
subsection.paragraph: The 2-level downgrade for multiple high-RoB domains follows GradePro guidance. The explanation string is surfaced in the UI so reviewers see why certainty moved.
